analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health service providing free comprehensive care to everyone in the country.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from October 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the private health insurance system with a United States Health Service — a new government agency that would employ salaried doctors, nurses, and other health workers, run its own hospitals and clinics, and provide all medical care free of charge to every person in the United States. It would be financed by new taxes on individuals, estates and trusts, and corporations, and by redirecting existing Medicare payroll taxes. It also guarantees paid leave from work to get health care, covers abortion and contraception services, sets up patient grievance systems, and puts patients and health workers on the boards that govern local facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person in the United States, including the more than 40 million the bill's findings say lacked coverage, would get comprehensive care — doctor visits, hospital care, dental, vision, mental health, prescriptions, long-term care — with no charge and no discrimination based on income, health status, or employment. Displaced health industry workers get hiring preference in the new Service, and existing health workers get a guaranteed job offer. Health workers gain union rights including the right to strike, card-check union recognition, and whistleblower protection for reporting poor care.

how_it_helps.text: All individuals in the United States are declared eligible for health care and supplemental services, provided without charge and without discrimination, with no exclusions for pre-existing conditions [S2][S3].

The Service must provide a broad benefit package including primary and specialty care, dental, vision, mental health, prescription drugs, long-term care, home health, ambulance transport, and child care during appointments [S2][S3].

The bill spells out enforceable patient rights: free choice of provider and facility, informed consent, confidentiality, translated materials, access to user advocates, and a grievance and legal-assistance system [S3].
Workers earn one hour of paid 'health leave' for every 35 hours worked, usable when they or a dependent need health care [S3].
Reproductive services including family planning, contraception, and abortion are provided without coercion and without prior approval of anyone other than the patient [S3].

The Service must redistribute resources to underserved inner-city, rural, minority, migrant, and prisoner populations, and its local governing boards are majority-controlled by patients, with workers also represented [S2][S3].

Health workers get federal labor-law coverage, card-check union recognition in place of elections, and the right to strike; people who join the Service get student loans paid off over four years of employment [S3].
The bill bars people with financial conflicts of interest from serving on health boards and requires full financial disclosure and an Inspector General to police the system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: New percentage surcharges on individual income taxes and on corporate income taxes, plus taxes on estates and trusts, fund a new Health Service Trust Fund, supplemented by the existing Medicare payroll taxes and a direct government contribution [S2][S3]. The health insurance industry's core business is eliminated — its administrative and sales workers are eligible for only limited retraining funds. For-profit hospitals, private practices that bill for services, and drug and equipment companies lose their pricing power and fee-for-service revenue: care is delivered by salaried employees of a public service, and private delivery of health care for payment outside the Service is barred [S3].

drawbacks.text: The financing burden would be enormous: the bill funds universal care with percentage surcharges on individual and corporate income taxes plus Medicare payroll taxes and a large direct government contribution, a cost every taxpayer and business would feel [S2][S3].

The transition eliminates private health insurance and converts providers to salaried public employees, and the bill budgets only up to 1 percent of the Service's first two annual budgets to retrain and rehire displaced insurance and administrative workers — far less than the scale of displacement [S3].

Doctors and other professionals could no longer collect fees or practice privately for payment outside the Service, which critics of single-payer plans argue would drive some providers out or abroad and risk waiting lists [S3].
Students at the new tuition-free health team schools must commit to at least two years of Service employment in regions the Board assigns, with financial penalties for breaking the agreement [S3].

The bill concentrates sweeping power — facility siting, staffing, a national drug formulary, clinical decision criteria, even eminent domain over real estate — in a 21-member presidentially appointed National Health Board, a governance design with few checks beyond disclosure rules and an Inspector General [S3].

The Service is exempted from some federal labor provisions — supervisors are covered by union law and the Board may impose settlement terms in regional health disputes — and patients' main remedy if the Service fails is reimbursement under the old Medicare rules, not a private lawsuit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have extended free, comprehensive care to every resident — the largest single expansion of health access ever proposed in Congress at the time — and eliminated premiums, deductibles, and medical debt. But it did this by abolishing the private health insurance industry and converting most of medicine to salaried public employment, financed by substantial new taxes, with a five-year buildup of public facilities and schools. The trade-off was real either way: no one without care pays again, but every taxpayer and the entire health sector absorbs the change at once, and the plan gave an appointed board enormous operational control with limited recourse if delivery fell short.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, then passed down to subcommittees, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on October 10, 2001 [S1][S5].
The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — for the parts falling under each panel's jurisdiction [S5].
In November 2001 it was referred to the Health subcommittees of two of those committees, and in March 2002 to the Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections subcommittees [S5].

No hearing, mark-up, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill's last recorded action is the March 27, 2002 subcommittee referral, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health system — insurers, for-profit hospitals and managed-care companies, and drug and equipment suppliers — kept its market and revenue stream, and taxpayers were spared the new surtaxes. The roughly 40 million uninsured people the bill cited gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health industry kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the single-payer national health service bill in the House.

against.name: Committee chairs of Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral (all Republicans in the 107th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in subcommittee after referral.

against.name: Health insurance, for-profit hospital, and pharmaceutical industries
against.role: Industries whose business the bill would eliminate or convert to public employment
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer national health service proposals of this era, which would have abolished private insurance and capped drug and provider payment; no industry activity on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; in a House with 223 Republicans and 208 Democrats, a bill with nine Democratic sponsors had no path to a committee vote, and the record shows no member besides the sponsor and cosponsors taking any action on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill eliminates employer and individual health insurance as the financing channel: its findings attack for-profit managed care, its trust fund replaces premiums, and existing employer health plans are wound down (Sec. 503). Insurance-industry administrative and sales workers are eligible for retraining out of a fund capped at 1 percent of the Service's budget in its first two years [S3].

Hospitals would be established and run by the public Service with salaried staff, and private delivery of health care for payment outside the Trust Fund is barred for decision-makers; the bill's findings target 'unnecessary and excessive profits' and for-profit managed care as inflating costs [S3].

Drugs, devices, and supplies would be distributed through a National Pharmacy and Medical Supply Formulary run by the Health Service, replacing the current market with a government purchasing channel — a direct loss of pricing power [S3].

industries.industry: Private-practice physicians and other fee-for-service health professionals
industries.note: Professionals would become salaried federal-style employees barred from outside fees, but they get a guaranteed job offer, civil service protections, union rights including card check and the right to strike, and repayment of educational loans over four years of Service employment [S3].
Existing employer-employee health plans are wound down, freeing employers of benefit costs, but corporations pay a new percentage income-tax surcharge to fund the Service [S2][S3].
